metadata.title: Pedagogical practices and civic knowledge and engagement in Latin America: Multilevel analysis using ICCS data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 microdata with a two-stage sampling design (schools selected first, then students/teachers within schools). For student-level analyses, the authors apply a “within-school student weight” computed as the product of class- and student-level weight factors (WGTFAC2S × WGTADJ2S × WGTADJ3S), and for school-level analyses they apply a “school weight” derived from WGTFAC1 and WGTADJ1S (and WGTFAC1 × WGTADJ1T for teacher-level analyses). The authors also note that, per the ICCS user guide, weights should be normalized so that the sum of weights equals the sample size, which is important for unbiased multilevel estimates under the complex design. No replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported in the provided text, so uncertainty estimation is described only at the multilevel-model level rather than via explicit replicate procedures.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable (ICCS Civic Knowledge and Engagement, SCKE) is based on five plausible values, and the authors state that all five plausible values were included in the analysis. However, the manuscript does not describe how missing questionnaire/test responses were handled (e.g., whether cases with missing predictors were excluded or whether any imputation was used), which is a reporting gap because ICCS datasets typically contain item nonresponse. As a result, the exact analytic sample for each model and the missing-data mechanism cannot be verified from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic dataset is ICCS 2016 for five Latin American and Caribbean countries (Chile, Colombia, Peru, Dominican Republic, Mexico). The target population is 13–14-year-old students in eighth grade (or ninth grade where the average age in eighth grade is <13.5 years), along with their teachers for the relevant grade. The paper does not report additional exclusions (e.g., complete-case rules for specific predictors, booklet-level restrictions beyond the ICCS balanced rotated design, or any missing-data filtering), so the filtering criteria beyond restricting to these five countries and the ICCS grade target cannot be further specified from the provided text.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 (target grade 8/9) — Civic Knowledge and Engagement (SCKE) cognitive test
main_findings.target_variable: Civic Knowledge and Engagement (SCKE) score (Plausible Values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear modeling (HLM8) with multilevel null model: ICC = 0.23 (χ2(119)=309.24, p<0.001). Model fit metrics beyond ICC are not reported; results are reported as regression coefficients (b) with t-tests and p-values by country.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 (target grade 8/9) the study leveraged civic learning at school (S_CIVLRN), openness in classroom discussions (OPDISC), civic participation in the wider community (S_COMPART), expected education level (S_ISCED), and home literacy resources (S_HOMLIT) to explain Civic Knowledge and Engagement (SCKE) plausible-value scores, finding that civic learning and classroom openness were positively associated with civic knowledge in several countries while wider-community civic participation was consistently negatively associated. This indicates that strengthening in-class civic learning and open discussion practices may improve civic knowledge, whereas encouraging broad community political participation may require careful alignment with students’ academic time and support to avoid trade-offs, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This Heliyon study analyzes ICCS 2016 data from five Latin American and Caribbean countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru) for the target grade (8th grade or 9th where applicable). The dependent variable is ICCS Civic Knowledge and Engagement (SCKE), measured via a cognitive test and represented using five plausible values that are included in the multilevel models. The authors use hierarchical linear modeling (HLM8) after estimating a null model, reporting an intraclass correlation of ICC = 0.23 (χ2(119)=309.24, p<0.001), indicating substantial between-school variation. Across countries, openness in classroom discussions and civic learning at school show positive associations with SCKE in multiple settings, while civic participation in the wider community is negatively associated. The paper reports regression coefficients (b) and country-specific t-tests rather than predictive ML metrics, and it does not document missing-data handling, limiting transparency about the analytic sample construction.
